facts.fact: Ward-stones: grey narrow standing stones taller than a mounted rider, older than the track, runes cut deep and filled with faint gold. They hum low (felt in the teeth), warm from the inside, the same at noon and midnight.
Horses raised at the wards sidestep once, then stand calm beside a stone.
Wardens read stones with lenses; Sylvanas reads by bare palm.
Two rings of stones: outer and second. A loaf-sized ward-stone sits inside the Pass cell, humming.
Ward-lamps give steady white-blue light as bright as noon.

A slate dampening plate carved in close lines suppresses a staff's crystal (dull violet, bruise-coloured); light goes flat within a hand's width. Taking the staff off it, the violet drains and the crystal's own pale colour returns.
Kirin Tor ink dries violet at the edges; Farstrider ink dries black.

Jaina's staff: ash, silver-wire grip, hen's-egg crystal. Staff reacts to contamination: hum in the wrist bones, the crystal buzzes in its claws, shivers pointing toward the strongest source; listening down it with the heel on the ground gives the currents back.
A flat grey pebble cut with one rune, in a twist of cloth: half of a pair; the twin sits in Antonidas's study. Quiet since Dalaran.

A wedge-shaped gold-runed damper stone set in a notch below the cell ward-stone presses on a held mage's chest like a flat hand and stops her reaching for her magic; removal lets the full noise of the currents in.
Leylines: currents magic runs along under the ground; stones are tied into them. Jaina senses them as a field of sound through the floor; every line in the Pass 'going at once'.

The contamination: sour late drag at the tail of each pulse; old-coin taste in the mouth; reads like death, 'necromancy' (a discipline nobody in Dalaran is taught); lattice and sequence of drag; holds together across leagues of line as though taught to travel; muffled inside the ward rings (a hand over an ear), loud outside them; in clay, groundwater, hedge roots, hawthorn; in crops (cabbage, beans, turnips rotting); in living animals (filmed milk-white eyes, bleeding from the nose, kept moving after a heart-shot; liver, lungs, blood and meat); horses read clean. Not in the elves' ability to feel directly.
A body that simply died carries a flat cold mark laid on from outside; the contamination runs through tissue like roots through a pot and grows over a long time, in life.

Jaina's deep palm-read goes down through crust, clay, water, roots and stone to the line; it costs her sensation in the hand and frost grows round her palm (a hand's width, going grey). Her frost cast through the staff glazes a stretch of road with white ice that cracks and freezes a wolf's hind feet.
The Kirin Tor have a long grace/process of agreeing what to call a thing before sending someone.

Elves cannot feel the contamination ('Nothing in the hide or the bones of her hand. There never was.'); the staff in Sylvanas's hand buzzes in her bones but tells her nothing. Thalassian horses are bred to tolerate ward hum and settle; in Millhaven her mare backs with ears pinned and blows hard, and three other horses spook (Neral's calms hers, Lyriel brings the mage's mare round).

The contamination is in Millhaven's well water ('thinner than in the doe'), the soil, the cellar, the footprints of the dead (heavier than the ground round them; cattle, dogs, hares and wheel ruts read light), the stone storehouse by the mill (the loudest place, louder than the crossing), the inn cellar and the mill, but the mage will not call the storehouse the origin ('a store is where things end up'). Footprints are heavier than their surroundings. The crossing read: all lines heavy; two heavier far out than under the crossing; the two north lines lag by distance; east does not lag; west drowned out; no source or sink verdict.

Frost from a deep read can tear skin off a hand when the hand is pulled up; at the storehouse it spreads further than at the well. A hand can lose its fine control for days ('curled halfway and stopped, stiff as a dead bird's foot').
Horses remain clean despite walking through it all day and drinking from the culvert stream (re-checked at night, staff-heel and cheek to the wood). Unexplained.
South of Millhaven the contamination reads wider and more spread out ('A stain in a cloth that's been wet through'), not a knot; at the noon crossing the crystal ticks nearly to a hum.

The dead of Millhaven rose after death (the girl's mam died and 'got up in the dark') and walked out on their own feet; the footprints are bare or clogged; deep, constant-depth toe-down grooves, four and five abreast; they leave the village by gates pushed from the inside out.

Diagnostic light: Jaina says 'the word for light, the plain one, the first every apprentice in the Violet Citadel learned' and sends it down the staff 'water down a rope'; the crystal goes pale gold and lights a body from inside so organs, vessels and pulse are visible; the contamination shows brown ('ink let fall into a glass of water'). Works through blankets and cloth with the crystal held against the body and her cheek on the ash; the light can be sent out along the arms and gut. Costs her a cold in the face and hands (the staff 'going cold under her cheek').

Holding ward: the first ward an apprentice learns, taught in the Dalaran alchemy rooms for glassware ('you put it round a flask that had to go into the furnace so it would not crack, and it did nothing to whatever was boiling inside'). Cast over a living body as a cold clean blue mesh ('the shadow side of snow'); it takes the contamination's drag on each pulse like a line holding a tug, stops further spread and calms a seizing patient to sleep; it does not cure. It stands by itself for hours and thins; it must be fed and trimmed by rounds; each costs a cold up the ash into her elbow and chest and into the roots of her teeth. Jaina had never put it round a person before.

Frost cast on a person: pins a man at the knees and a free hand to a floor and post with white feathering frost; thaws into his boots; he has no feeling in his legs for a while. The frost cast returns up the staff into her left hand (linen turns 'hard as card').

Shell ward: a hard blue dome pressed flat to the boards ('a bowl dropped over a candle'), edges biting into wood with a hiss, fumes lying under it like smoke under glass; held from dusk to first light with nobody putting a foot on it; costs her a tear in the left palm and an arm 'ice from the fingers to the shoulder'.

The built contamination: in a sealed clay jar (waxed cloth over the mouth) it is a dark substance darker than oil with a skin forming like cooling jam, smelling of pears gone brown and, beneath, a struck flint; it spreads along the grain of boards in thin dark fingers. It is a stack of at least three spells laid on one another: one part to keep, one to wait, one she cannot follow. In flour it goes through a baker's oven and into the eater, where it sits and waits; it is the same thing as in the doe, Garran, the Millhaven well, but whole (in the sick it is thin and smeared). It is written in the necromantic (death-currents) grammar; Jaina can feel the structure but cannot read its meaning.

Staging of the sickness in a person: early (a day or two): fever flush, sweet pear breath, a fist or smaller knot under the breastbone and a thread along the gut, nothing in blood, lungs, arms or head; late (weeks of daily dose): everywhere (liver swollen and dark, lungs, great vessels, down both arms to the fingers), every thread running back to the gut; breath 'meat kept too long'; belly round and hard. Dose is cumulative; stopping the dose lets early cases recover (cool forehead by dawn); wards hold the rest.

Jaina tells death-currents craft from other magic by its signs; flour dust hanging in lamp air is an explosion risk (mill explosions at Boralus). Water carries only a little ('thin, a hair's weight on the tail of each beat'). Tam, who guarded but never ate the flour, was clean.

In the village the contamination is 'thin and spread and moving' through the living; the currents under the cobbles run their slow pulse with a late weight on each beat. In the granary the drag 'ground', 'one long pull' up the ash.

Jaina reads contamination on a road from a mile-post or crossing and grades it: heavy/light, old (settled in the ground) vs starting (thin, new). North, west and south roads old and heavy, east light and starting; the King's road thin and clean (a smear where carts that were near it passed). She cannot hear places she has not visited ('I haven't been there').

Jaina cannot read paper, books or people: the burned slips carry nothing ('It never sat by any of it'); the overseer carries nothing ('No more than on you'); an emptied store leaves residue 'like a room where somebody's smoked a pipe for years, after you've opened the windows'.

Reading costs Jaina: the staff's crystal runs a washed-out gold, dimmer through the day; cold comes into rooms with her (a draught); teeth chatter and frost rises on bare fingertips; at the fork the crystal's light 'leaned' toward the contaminated road. Sylvanas holding the staff feels 'a cold stick hum in her bones and mean nothing'.
Jaina's right arm remains dead (staff carried in the crook), left hand wrapped with two usable fingertips for writing and knots.

Chapter 6: the contamination reads through staff and horse as a 'dull drag' under the road with a late hitch behind every pulse; it rises hard where a stream runs under the road (culvert), grows with each farm lane that joins the south road, and becomes overwhelming in the walled approach to Andorhal and over the city ('beat on, slow and late'). Jaina feels it in the roots of her teeth from the rise.

Chapter 6: Jaina's cost ladder: staff crystal 'straw left in the rain' dipping with the pulse; at Andorhal's approach pressure like diving deep, ears hurting, teeth chattering in the heat, white frost on the bare fingertips creeping over the linen, the crystal sinking until she can see the grain of the stone, and a nosebleed.

Chapter 6: the plague model Jaina states: a single distributed system with a keeping part that holds the substance whole through mill, oven and gut, accumulating with each meal, killing when enough has gathered, then the body walking. She cannot read or explain the last step.

Chapter 6: Dalaran's library has a locked grille over death-current books; first-years get the warnings and the spines, and a master tells them the art is 'keeping a body useful after the person in it had gone'. Kirin Tor design principle: lay a ward with every seam closed, nothing loose for the next spell to catch on. Antonidas is the reader of her write-ups.

Chapter 6: Jaina's sense reads residue off things that have sat with the grain and off ground and horses, but she cannot read people (a tired clerk is just a clerk) and has not tried turning the staff on a man on the road.

Chapter 7: Jaina's sample-room reads classify sealed grain bags as 'heavy' (contaminated) or 'clean'; every bag on a copied mark is heavy, bags on true marks are clean. The cost of a day of reads: grey face, hoarse voice, dead staff crystal, frost on the linen on a warm night, two white fingertips. She cannot write (blots) and 'can't hear paper'.

Chapter 7: the contamination is a thin coat applied by hand to grain after dressing and before the sack is sewn, worked in so every grain gets some; alone it does little; what it carries wakes only inside whoever eats the bread. Whoever filled the crock knows alchemy and necromancy. Handlers wear waxed cloths and long gloves and wash to the elbow; whatever is on the gloves can kill the man inside them. A residue is 'wet' and readable for a night; once gloves are burned and boards swilled she gets only sacks.
Chapter 7: Jaina proposes to freeze a living man's jaw with a fingertip touch before he can bite his collar, once tonight (not yet shown).
Chapter 7: the sample room and copy room at the Kirin Tor inspection office open to a magister's ring or tags.
